subject: item parameter estimates obtained from mirt()

messages.author: b9bf80c091ea12e4
messages.subject: item parameter estimates obtained from mirt()
parts:
Hi Phil,

I am using mirt package to study parameter linking methods, thanks for your contribution, this package helps me a lot. Recently I got some enquires about item parameters estimation by mirt():
 
As shown in the code below, I sampled two groups of examinees from latent trait distribution N(0, 1) and N(0.5, 1.2^2) respectively, then simulated responses of these two groups and got the corresponding parameter estimates of common items by mirt(). Theoretically, for the estimates obtained by marginal maximum likelihood method with standard restrictions, the high able group should have a negative shift in threshold parameter estimates, due to higher mean scores. But the results I obtained is kind of weird, which is just the opposite, the N(0.5, 1.2^2) group even produced larger threshold parameter estimates. 

Part of Code
# simulate responses for Test X
# ability distribution N(0,1)
n <- 500
Theta_X <- rnorm(n,0,1)
X_responses <- simdata(a= a_common , d=b_ common, N=n, itemtype="graded", Theta=Theta_X)
# simulate responses for Test Y
# ability distribution N(0.5,1.2)
Theta_Y <- rnorm(n,0.5,1.2)
Y_responses <- simdata(a=a_common, d=b_ common, N=n, itemtype="graded", Theta=Theta_Y)
itemstats(X_responses)
itemstats(Y_responses)

ex<-mirt(data=X_responses, model=1, itemtype="graded", SE=TRUE,
     SE.type="crossprod", method="EM", dentype="Gaussian")
ey<-mirt(data=Y_responses, model=1, itemtype="graded", SE=TRUE,
         SE.type="crossprod", method="EM", dentype="Gaussian")

Results 
coef(ex)[[1]]
               a1       d1         d2
par     0.70      1.65     -0.41

coef(ey)[[1]]
               a1       d1         d2
par     0.52     1.92       0.00

coef(ex)[[2]]
               a1        d1        d2
par     1.33     -0.03     -0.91

coef(ey)[[2]]
               a1        d1         d2
par     1.28     0.64      -0.44


I suspected that I did not set the proper parameters for mirt() function, so what I got was actually not MMLE. But I haven't figured out the problem yet. Here are some questions I think may be relevant:

1. Is the estimation method by default marginal maximum likelihood?

2. For dentype: 'Gaussian' (default) assumes a multivariate Gaussian distribution with an
associated mean vector and variance-covariance matrix. Is the "associated mean vector and variance-covariance matrix" by default standard restrictions?

3. Any parameter I should use but did not include in my code?

Thank you very much!
Nanxi

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: item parameter estimates obtained from mirt()
parts:
The setup looks correct to me, though note that ey is not on the same scale as ex due to the mean-var shift in the trait distribution (hence, the need for equating, which can be done via the plink package [e.g., https://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/html/read.mirt.html] or using the multipleGroup() function for concurrent equating). 

Regarding your questions:
1. Is the estimation method by default marginal maximum likelihood?
Yes, and if item prior distributions are included this becomes marginal maximum a posteriori.

2. For dentype: 'Gaussian' (default) assumes a multivariate Gaussian distribution with an
associated mean vector and variance-covariance matrix. Is the "associated mean vector and variance-covariance matrix" by default standard restrictions?
Yes, and most often set to 0-1.
3. Any parameter I should use but did not include in my code?

Looks fine to me as this is the building blocks for many equating algorithms.

Phil

Thank you very much!
Nanxi

Hi Oxana,

On Sun, Aug 25, 2024 at 10:53 PM Oxana Rosca <oxan...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Phil,

Thank you for the mirt package and your informative responses. 

I've got similar results but without group comparison. I work with multistage testing reading assessment that was developed for high-school students. My sample was 4,500 undergraduate students, and the assessment seemed expectedly easy for them. The item pool consisted of 30 6-item passages/testlets. Each student responded to 3 randomly chosen passages (18 items). Every passage was responded to by 400-500 students. The boxplot of mean values in the attached file shows that three-quarters of 180 items were responded to correctly by 75% or more of the students who got them. However, all but one location parameter (b-parameter or d-parameter) estimated by the bifactor 2PL model are positive. The 169 items ranged from  -0.08 to 5.98 (the theta scale is -6, 6). Eleven items had location parameters between 6 and 18.6. 


The d parameters are intercepts, not the traditional difficulty parameter (b), so in that sense they are more akin to "easiness" parameters centered at the value when theta = 0 (cf. b values, which reflect the theta location where the response curve inflects, which is often at P(theta) = .5). So a number of high values makes sense in this context and indeed reflects the easiness of the item. If it helps, mirt has an interactive shiny interface to get accustomed to the parameterisations, which can be loaded via mirt::itemplot(shiny=TRUE) 
 

As I understand, such results suggest that the assessment was hard for the sample. Please help me with this puzzle.

My second question is about the a2-parameters (for specific factors/testlets). You mentioned in your other responses in this group that negative a2-parameters were OK since they are calculated as partial correlation coefficients via regression. You also mentioned that a-parameters with absolute values smaller than 0.1 could be excluded from the assessments because their inflection point is very far from the center of theta distribution, hence, they are too difficult for all respondents of the sample. Does the latter apply to a1-parameters and/or a2-parameters of the bifactor model?


In the context of a bifactor model the a2 parameter being small would indicate a weak partial correlation, so the specific factor has little influence over an item. In such cases you could consider dropping the loading as they would be unlikely to influence the measurement model's results. Note that small a's are not 'difficulty', they are just not very informative as the item is not really influence by changes in the defined latent trait (at least, as far as it is able to tell within the predictable scope of the model). HTH.

Phil
 

Thank you for your help,

Oxana
